You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Accepted stripe case

A fresh 28x28 test had full-width rows r0=5, r4=3, r20=7, with all other rows 0. Accepted output: 28 uniform rows in repeating cycle `[5,3,7]` from row 0. This was accepted after four valid but incorrect cycle guesses and one malformed submission. This is exact observed success, not a universal stripe-order rule.

## Fresh 20x20 diagonal test solved from demo evidence (2026-10)
Test had sparse multi-strand diagonal marks (colors 7,1,3,5) over bg0. Seven demos were requested; the decisive demo 7 (7x7) had sparse diagonal 3/9 marks and output a dense texture with period four along anti-diagonal index `r+c`: every output cell depends only on `(r+c) mod 4`. Its row0 was `[9,3,3,9,9,3,3]`; rows continue the same anti-diagonal pattern, shifting phase each row. The solved test output was a full 20x20 texture with anti-diagonal period 4 and sequence `[5,3,7,1]` indexed by `r+c mod 4`, i.e. `out[r][c] = [5,3,7,1][(r+c)%4]`. This was accepted. The sequence can be read directly from test's top-left 7 marker at (0,2), corresponding sum-index 2 ->7; color 1 on anti-diagonal at row4 col19 (sum23, mod4=3) fixes 1; color 3 on anti-diagonal sum29 (mod4=1) fixes 3; color 5 on sum32 (mod4=0) fixes 5. Thus the marks establish phase and palette sequence `[5,3,7,1]`. Do not assume sequence maps input colors directly; anti-diagonal colors are calibration marks, and the sparse input's actual marked cells are consistent with periodic texture hypothesis.

Practical discriminator: when sparse diagonal tracks occur and a demo shows complete output constant on `r+c` diagonals, test for a short anti-diagonal period, then infer values/order and phase from demo coordinates and test marker constraints. In this solved instance period 4 was supported by demo7's repeating 4-wide anti-diagonal pattern; other task-44bebe54 geometry variants (full-width row-stripes) follow different rules. Do not apply diagonal pattern to stripe-only inputs or infer this sequence universally.

Task ID also has diagonal-marker periodic-texture variants; classify geometry first. Stripe demos in this instance had varied cycles not trivially source-order, first-occurrence unique colors, or sorted colors: `[2,8,5]`, `[9,9,1,7,6,4]`, `[8,4,7,9,1]`, `[3,4,7,7,1,4]`, `[6,5]`. Do not infer a universal permutation law from `[5,3,7]`.

## Fresh multi-strand recurrence (2026-10, unresolved; eight wrong submissions)
Test 19x19, bg0. Sparse anti-diagonal line palette: color 1 on r+c=3; color 8 on r+c=9..17 (segment); color 9 on r+c=19..29 (segment); color 6 on r+c=24..35 (segment); color 4 has short/paired appearances including r+c=27,29,31,33,35,37; color2 at r+c=34,36. Geometry overlaps in anti-diagonal sum bands, with some lines represented by multiple colors/segments. Eight rejected full-grid periodic guesses included palettes [1,8,9,6,4,2], both r+c and c-r indexing, and variants replacing initial 1 with 9. None is validated; do not repeat them.

Eight demos in that instance were highly heterogeneous: (1) 12x12 diagonal tracks became 2D period-6 stripe-like output, row0 cycle [3,2,6,6,4,8]; (2) 29x29 all-zero with a long diagonal 2 yielded solid 2 everywhere; (3) 22x22 colored diagonal tracks output 2D period-4 pattern with row0 [9,5,6,8]; (4) 28x28 diagonal strands output period-4 pattern with row0 [6,8,3,6] (equivalently phase shifts by row); (5) 6x6 diagonal tracks output period-3 pattern row0 [9,9,4,9,9,4]; (6) full-width stripes output row sequence periodic [7,6,5,9] with duplicated 7; (7) diagonal motif/strands output 2D period-5 row0 [4,2,2,2,8] (with 4/8 and background-color 2); (8) full-width row stripes generated repeating sequence [2,8,1,4,1]. These make clear task ID covers several encoding variants; no one cycle/permutation was derived for this test.

Lesson: each demo may encode its own underlying rule class; identify relation from exact strand geometry and output before guessing. The 19x19 test remains unresolved; no safe answer inferred.

If applying this accepted pattern as a hypothesis on recurrence, validate the actual instance with demos. Check exact output height/row widths: one previous attempt was invalid due to serialization dimensions. A 17x17 diagonal-strand demo in this instance expanded to a periodic texture with period-seven diagonal sequence `[3,7,4,6,9,5,2]`; do not apply stripe-only logic to diagonal inputs.

# Continual-ARC Interaction Discipline

Use alongside `continual-arc-solving` for interactive ARC benchmarks with costly demo and submission actions.

## Turn protocol
- Each response must contain exactly one permitted action JSON object on the last line; if JSON-only is required, emit no surrounding prose.
- Use only an action allowed by the benchmark. Do not call unrelated tools or issue scratch actions during a constrained puzzle turn.
- Track demo and wrong-submission budgets; each action has a score cost.

## Evidence loop
1. Parse the task and available examples. Form concrete competing hypotheses where ambiguity remains.
2. Request a demo only when its possible outcomes would discriminate between those hypotheses at worthwhile expected cost.
3. Once a demo arrives, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changes and invariants, then update the hypothesis before acting again.
4. Validate a candidate against every available demo and the fresh test input before submission. Preserve unchanged cells and verify dimensions.
5. Submit when the transformation is supported; request further demos only to resolve a stated uncertainty. Finish only when the instance permits it.

## Pitfalls
- Never spend repeated demo requests without analyzing the newest returned pair first.
- A remembered task ID or prior solution is a hypothesis, not a substitute for fresh-instance evidence.
- For task-27c7d27a, a validated recurrence recolors to 2 the union of every row and column monochromatic in the untouched input, regardless of that line's hue; preserve all cells outside the union. Check complete lines before edits.
